messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

On a gray August afternoon in 2023, James—21, recently married, living with his partner—was in the kitchen when a scream rang through the hallway. A friend from a local community group had crashed her motorcycle, skidding into the back window of their building. James ran to the stairwell, the sound of splintered glass filling his ears. The impact of her blood left a echo in his mind. In the days that followed, he noticed subtle cues that set his heart racing: a stranger passing by with a furtive glance, a neighbor commenting on his sister's recent surgery, and any sight of a wrist or broken collarbone, all of which triggered an instinctive urge to withdraw. When a suspicious passerby appeared, James instinctively stopped the program he was watching, a first sign that the triggers were pushing him toward maladaptive strategies. The sudden movements of people around him raised a feeling of threat that made his chest tighten; even the faint smell of gasoline could trigger a flashback, and the memory of the event returned as a vivid photograph in his mind. Over the next weeks, James's internal dialogue hardened. He convinced himself that his body was a battlefield: a whisper that his heart would race again, that the sight of a wrist might be a threat. He no longer felt capable of handling the ordinary tasks that once defined his confidence. When he heard the neighbor comment about his sister's surgery, he saw the remark as a deliberate probe, a reminder that his loved ones could still be hurt. This belief that he could not rely on himself amplified his sensitivity to perceived suspiciousness, turning even harmless gestures—an outstretched hand or a brief look—into triggers that set off a cascade of panic. James's memory of the accident remained intrusive. The scent of the spilled blood lingered whenever he passed a store with fresh perfume, and the shape of a broken wrist was etched so clearly that he could not find words to describe the terror. Whenever the smell rose, he pulled his phone and deleted any videos or news articles, avoiding media that might flood his senses with similar images. This avoidance was his first maladaptive strategy. At the same time, the vividness of the memory reinforced his belief that his body was perpetually on guard, a constant reminder that danger lurked, bolstering his negative appraisal that he could no longer rely on himself. The threat he felt was immediate and tangible. Every sudden movement by a stranger seemed like an imminent attack; a door slamming shut felt like a scream behind the wall. In response, James would stop all television, even if the show had no violence. He fled the apartment and found himself in crowded coffee shops where he could not be alone. When the threat of being in a quiet room rose, he would lash his wrists with a pen, a desperate attempt to let the pain out of his mind. Each episode of perceived threat sharpened his negative appraisal that he had lost control of his body, and it also made ordinary movements—like a colleague passing by—feel like new triggers of danger. James's avoidance habits had locked him into a cycle that brought his daily life to a grinding halt. By avoiding media, he missed the chance to process memories that might otherwise have faded. Yet on rare occasions when he slipped—perhaps watching a crime documentary on a friend's suggestion—he found the memory surge back with such force that it felt like a second accident. The sudden images pushed him into heightened threat, prompting him to retreat again, self-harm, and avoid being alone. That act of self-harm, a maladaptive strategy, intensified the sense of danger, so even routine steps toward a door felt like new triggers. His constant guard seeped into his marriage; his partner noted his growing distance over trivial misunderstandings. At 21, unemployed, he recognizes his safety net frayed. The decision to seek therapy comes from a place of fear: he fears the loop will crush his marriage and strip him of control, and he hopes to quiet the relentless voice inside his head that tells him his body is forever under attack.
